answer_text:
Let \(X=A^{-1}B\). Then \(B=AX\) and

\[
X^{-1}=B^{-1}A.
\]

Given

\[
A^{-1}+B^{-1}=(A+B)^{-1},
\]

multiply on the right by \(A+B\):

\[
(A^{-1}+B^{-1})(A+B)=I.
\]

Expanding,

\[
I+A^{-1}B+B^{-1}A+I=I,
\]

so

\[
A^{-1}B+B^{-1}A=-I.
\]

In terms of \(X\),

\[
X+X^{-1}=-I.
\]

Multiply by \(X\):

\[
X^2+I=-X
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
X^2+X+I=0.
\]

Thus

\[
(X-I)(X^2+X+I)=X^3-I=0,
\]

so

\[
X^3=I.
\]

Taking determinants,

\[
(\det X)^3=1.
\]

Also,

\[
\det B=\det(AX)=\det A\det X=-3\det X.
\]

Therefore \(\det B\) is \(-3\) times a cube root of unity.

If \(A\) and \(B\) are real matrices, then \(\det X\) is real, so \(\det X=1\). Hence

\[
\det B=-3.
\]

If complex matrices are allowed, then \(\det X\in\{1,\omega,\omega^2\}\), where \(\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}\), giving possible values

\[
-3,\quad -3\omega,\quad -3\omega^2.
\]

\[
\boxed{-3\text{ (real matrices); complex case: }-3,\,-3\omega,\,-3\omega^2}
\]
